title: Ice Cream 1.5L

drivers.name: Price increase (2.3%)
drivers.evidence: Historical: 2 weeks at $6.56 show median x0.54 vs baseline; noise-adjusted estimate x0.65. One past price hike at same level.

drivers.name: Competitor store opening
drivers.evidence: New competitive threat; no prior data, but plausible demand loss. Low confidence, so shrink effect.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 44.1. No event or promotion is planned. The price increased 2.3% to $6.56, which historically correlates with a 32% sales drop (2026-09-28: 24 units vs baseline 44.1, x0.54). A competitor opening across the street introduces demand loss risk. Past price hikes at $6.56 (2026-09-28, 2026-10-05) show median x0.54 vs baseline. The noise-adjusted effect of price increases is x0.65. The competitor entry is a new, untested risk with weak evidence. Combined, these reduce the median. The uplift model suggests no effect, but judgment overrides this due to price and competitive threat. Evidence is moderate, so shrink toward 1.0.

brief:
PRODUCT: Ice Cream 1.5L | category Frozen | Store #12 (Austin, TX)
TARGET WEEK: 2026-11-30 to 2026-12-06 (8 weeks after the last week with sales data)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 6.56 (+2.3% vs regular price 6.41)
  planner notes: A competitor opens a store across the street this week

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 44.1 | 5%-95%: 10.5 - 75.8 | 10%-90%: 19.4 - 71.2

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-36% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
